lead: A generative adversarial network (GAN) learns to make new data by playing a game. A generator G turns random noise z into a fake sample G(z). A discriminator D looks at real data x and fake samples and outputs a probability that its input is real. G tries to fool D; D tries to tell them apart. Training alternates between the two. GANs are used for face and product image synthesis, image-to-image translation, and data augmentation. They often give sharper images than VAEs, but training is less stable.
prereq: You need: 6.2 for latent variables and likelihood, Unit 2 for gradient-based optimization, and Unit 3 for CNN layers used in image GANs.

blocks.text: The generator G(z; θ_g) maps a noise vector z ~ p_z to a fake sample. θ_g are the generator weights. Typical z is 100 random numbers from a normal or uniform distribution. The discriminator D(x; θ_d) maps a sample x to a scalar probability in [0, 1], usually after a sigmoid. θ_d are the discriminator weights. For images, both are CNNs: G uses upsampling or transpose convolutions, and D uses strided convolutions. G never sees real data directly; it learns only from D's gradients. D sees both real and fake data.

blocks.where: V is the value of the game; D(x) is the probability D gives to real x; G(z) is the fake sample; p_data is the real data distribution; p_z is the noise distribution; E is expectation; log is natural log.

blocks.text: D wants high D(x) and low D(G(z)), so D maximizes V. G wants high D(G(z)), so G minimizes V. With one real and one fake sample, V = log D(real) + log(1 − D(fake)). For fixed G, the best D is D*(x) = p_data(x) / (p_data(x) + p_g(x)), where p_g is the distribution of G(z). If p_g = p_data, then D*(x) = 1/2. Only a few universities ask you to derive this.

items: Sample m real examples x from the data and m noise vectors z from p_z.
Compute fake examples G(z). Keep G fixed and update D by ascending the gradient of (1/m)Σ[log D(x) + log(1 − D(G(z)))].
Sample fresh noise z. Keep D fixed and update G by descending the gradient of its own loss.
Repeat both updates for many iterations.

blocks.where: L_G is the non-saturating generator loss; D(G(z)) is the discriminator's probability that a fake sample is real; lower L_G means G is fooling D better.

blocks.text: Early in training, D can reject fakes easily, so D(G(z)) is near 0. The term log(1 − D(G(z))) then saturates near 0 and G's gradient vanishes. The non-saturating loss −log D(G(z)) avoids this flat region. It has the same fixed point as the minimax game but a stronger gradient. The two losses are not identical during training. D's output is a probability, not a hard label.

Mode collapse means G maps many different z to a few similar samples. D cannot force G to cover every mode of the data. This is not overfitting; it is a failure of the game. Instability is the other common problem. If D becomes too strong, G gets weak gradients. If D is too weak, G gets no useful signal. Careful learning rates, batch normalization, label smoothing, and extra D updates can help. GAN samples can be sharp, but judging sample quality is hard.

items: Conditional GAN: G(z, y) and D(x, y) both receive a class label y or text. This lets you ask for a specific digit or object class.
CycleGAN: two generators A→B and B→A plus two discriminators. A cycle loss ‖F(G(a)) − a‖₁ keeps content. It works on unpaired sets, such as horse↔zebra, not on paired before/after images.
Progressive GAN: start at low resolution, then add layers as training stabilizes, up to 1024×1024 faces. This makes high-resolution training more stable.

blocks.text: Image editing, inpainting, and super-resolution use GANs as conditional priors; see 6.6. Bias and deepfakes are ethical risks; see 6.7.

figure.caption: The discriminator scores real data and generator output; its score trains the generator, while its own weights update from the real and fake labels.

spec.title: GAN training loop
spec.aria: Noise goes to a generator that makes fake samples, and a discriminator compares fake and real samples.

examples.question: For one real sample x and one fake sample G(z), D(x) = 0.8 and D(G(z)) = 0.3. Compute the discriminator maximization objective V for this pair and the non-saturating generator loss. State whether G wants the loss lower or higher. Use natural log.
steps: G minimizes this loss, so lower is better. D(G(z)) closer to 1 gives lower L_G.
examples.answer: V ≈ −0.580 and the non-saturating generator loss L_G ≈ 1.204; G wants lower L_G.
examples.check:
import math
D_real = 0.8
D_fake = 0.3
V = math.log(D_real) + math.log(1 - D_fake)
G_loss = -math.log(D_fake)
print(round(V, 3))
print(round(G_loss, 3))

traps: Do not update the generator with the discriminator's real-data term; the generator sees only fake samples.
Do not flip the sign: D maximizes V, while G minimizes V or minimizes the non-saturating loss −log D(G(z)).
D output 0.5 does not mean training has failed; it means D cannot separate real from fake for that input.
Mode collapse is not overfitting. The generator has lost data modes; it is not memorizing training points.
CycleGAN is for unpaired data. Pix2pix-style paired translation is a different setting.

quiz.q: What does the discriminator output in a standard GAN?
quiz.a: A probability in [0, 1] that its input is real.

quiz.q: Why does D maximize V while G minimizes V?
quiz.a: D wants high D(x) and low D(G(z)), so it maximizes V. G wants high D(G(z)), so it minimizes V.

quiz.q: Given D(real) = 0.9 and D(fake) = 0.2, compute V and the non-saturating G loss. Use natural log.
Why can a very strong discriminator hurt generator learning early in training?
quiz.a: D(fake) becomes near 0, so log(1 − D(G(z))) saturates and G's gradient is small. The non-saturating loss reduces this problem.
G maps many different z values to a few similar outputs, so it covers only part of the data distribution.

quiz.q: In a conditional GAN for a digit 7 image, what extra input does D receive?
quiz.a: D receives the image x together with the label y: D(x, y). G receives z and y: G(z, y).

quiz.q: Compare CycleGAN and a paired image-to-image GAN.
quiz.a: CycleGAN uses two generators and two discriminators with a cycle-consistency loss for unpaired sets. A paired GAN uses matched input-output pairs as supervision.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of Progressive GAN?
quiz.a: Train at low resolution first, then add layers gradually to reach high resolution.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, GANs are used for synthetic training data, face generation, and image translation, while diffusion models now lead many image tasks. Evaluation uses metrics such as FID, and newer GAN variants use Wasserstein loss or style-based generators. Search terms: WGAN, StyleGAN, FID, conditional GAN, CycleGAN, progressive growing.
